initial_observation.demographics: 37-year-old Hispanic male patient native of Honduras
initial_observation.encounter_context: presented to his primary care physician
initial_observation.chief_complaint: subacute symptoms of episodic vertigo, nausea, left-sided tinnitus or “buzzing,” and hearing loss
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: subacute episodic vertigo, nausea, left-sided tinnitus, and hearing loss, exacerbated by dehydration and salty foods; neurological exam including cranial nerves and cerebellar function normal; dizziness on Hallpike maneuver without nystagmus; provisional diagnosis of left-sided Meniere’s disease
known_prior_history: episode of tapeworm infection as a teenager prior to immigrating to the USA

evidence_items.source_text: The neurological examination, including of the cranial nerves and cerebellar function, was normal. During the Hallpike maneuver, the patient reported dizziness, but no nystagmus was observed. Aside from a left nasal septal deviation, his physical examination was normal. He was provisionally diagnosed with left-sided MD and referred for electrocochleography (ECOG) and a vestibulonystagmogram (VNG).
His treatment included dietary and lifestyle modifications, along with oral steroids.

The patient’s laboratory testing results showed that both the complete blood count (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) were within normal limits. The C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 1 mg/L, which fell within the normal range of 0–10 mg/L. The sedimentation rate was 8 mm/hour, which was within the normal range of 0–15 mm/hour. Anticardiolipin antibody levels for immunoglobulin (Ig)A, IgG, and IgM were all less than 9 units, each within their respective normal ranges (IgA 0–11 anti phospolipid antibodies (APL) U/ml, IgG 0–14 GPL U/ml, and IgM 0–12 MPL U/ml). Similarly, beta-2 glycoprotein antibody levels for IgA, IgG, and IgM were all less than 9 units, well within their normal ranges (IgA 0–25 GPI IgA units, IgG 0–20 GPI IgG units, and IgM 0–32 GPI IgM units). Additionally, the Lyme IgG/IgM antibodies test was negative, as were the tests for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid arthritis factor. The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was 2.020 uIU/mL, within the normal range of 0.450–4.500 uIU/mL.

Additional imaging was ordered, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed postinflammatory calcifications in the right parietal lobe as well as generalized volume loss, which was more significant than expected for the patient’s age.
The patient tested positive for antibodies to heat shock proteins (anti-HSP).

An ECOG was obtained using a slow rate alternating click, presented at 70 dB HL in the right ear and 90 dB HL in the left ear, owing to unilateral hearing loss. Responses were averaged to approximately 1500–3000 sweeps. The sensitivity parameter (SP)/action potential (AP) ratios were averaged from the best three waveforms obtained. An SP/AP ratio of 50% or greater is considered abnormal. The SP/AP ratio on the right was 67.4%, and on the left it was 66.7%. The ECOG morphology was considered very good. Results were consistent with hydrops or increased perilymphatic pressure bilaterally (Fig. 1).

VNG testing revealed no significant gaze, spontaneous, or positional nystagmus. Both saccadic eye velocity and latency remained within normal ranges. However, visual pursuit appeared abnormal owing to low gain. Optokinetic tests were within normal limits on both sides. Additionally, the Dix-Hallpike test yielded negative results for both sides. Subclinical nystagmus was observed during head and body-left testing (less than 3 degrees of left-beating). Bithermal caloric irrigations suggested abnormal peripheral function, including a 57% weakness in the left ear.

The audiological evaluation revealed a significant low-frequency SNHL in the patient’s left ear, which persisted over time. Within a year, the patient also developed low-frequency hearing loss in the right ear (Figs. 2a and b). Such bilateral, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss is highly indicative of MD.
The MRI revealed a 3 mm postinflammatory calcification in the right parietal lobe, thus confirming a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis (Fig. 3).

His symptoms were reportedly exacerbated by dehydration and the ingestion of salty foods.
He was provisionally diagnosed with left-sided MD and referred for electrocochleography (ECOG) and a vestibulonystagmogram (VNG).
An ECOG was obtained ... Results were consistent with hydrops or increased perilymphatic pressure bilaterally.

The audiological evaluation revealed a significant low-frequency SNHL in the patient’s left ear, which persisted over time. Within a year, the patient also developed low-frequency hearing loss in the right ear. Such bilateral, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss is highly indicative of MD.

The ear, nose, and throat (ENT) physician suspected autoimmune sensorineural hearing loss secondary to the initial parasitic infection and referred the patient to a rheumatologist.
